claims.evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry analysis in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Both Nsp1 and Nsp14 are involved in the ability of SARS-CoV-2 to degrade host RNA and inhibit host protein translation.
claims.source: Both Nsp1 and Nsp14 are involved in the ability of SARS-CoV-2 to degrade host RNA (Nsp1), and inhibit host protein translation (Nsp1 and Nsp14), and these activities have been implicated in their ability to counteract the interferon response within the infected cell (Yuan et al., 2021; Hsu et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Yuan et al., 2021 and Hsu et al., 2021.

claims.claim: NK ligands are highly susceptible to inhibition of synthesis.
claims.source: Together with our biochemical analysis, this data suggests that NK ligands are highly susceptible to inhibition of synthesis, and that SARS-CoV-2 manipulation of host protein production could impact the NK response in addition to the interferon response.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the cycloheximide and Nsp1/Nsp14 experiments.

claims.claim: SARS-CoV-2 manipulation of host protein production could impact the NK response in addition to the interferon response.
claims.source: Together with our biochemical analysis, this data suggests that NK ligands are highly susceptible to inhibition of synthesis, and that SARS-CoV-2 manipulation of host protein production could impact the NK response in addition to the interferon response.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined biochemical and functional data.

claims.claim: Degranulation of CD3-CD56+ NK cells was significantly reduced against SARS-CoV-2 infected cells.
claims.source: To determine whether this was the case, we incubated SARS-CoV-2 infected cells with PBMC, and measured (i) degranulation of CD3-CD56+ NK cells (Figure 4C; Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), (ii) production of IFNγ (Figure 4D), and (iii) TNFα (Figure 4E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B). Consistent with data using other viruses Vlahava et al., 2021, CD107a was recirculated on a higher proportion of NK cells than IFNγ and TNFα. Nevertheless, all three markers of NK activation were significantly reduced in SARS-CoV-2 infected versus mock infected cells, suggesting that the virus has evolved to inhibit NK cell responses.
claims.evidence: This is shown by functional NK cell assays in Figures 4C-E.

claims.claim: Production of IFNγ by NK cells was significantly reduced against SARS-CoV-2 infected cells.
claims.source: To determine whether this was the case, we incubated SARS-CoV-2 infected cells with PBMC, and measured (i) degranulation of CD3-CD56+ NK cells (Figure 4C; Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), (ii) production of IFNγ (Figure 4D), and (iii) TNFα (Figure 4E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B). Consistent with data using other viruses Vlahava et al., 2021, CD107a was recirculated on a higher proportion of NK cells than IFNγ and TNFα. Nevertheless, all three markers of NK activation were significantly reduced in SARS-CoV-2 infected versus mock infected cells, suggesting that the virus has evolved to inhibit NK cell responses.
claims.evidence: This is shown by functional NK cell assays in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Production of TNFα by NK cells was significantly reduced against SARS-CoV-2 infected cells.
claims.source: To determine whether this was the case, we incubated SARS-CoV-2 infected cells with PBMC, and measured (i) degranulation of CD3-CD56+ NK cells (Figure 4C; Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), (ii) production of IFNγ (Figure 4D), and (iii) TNFα (Figure 4E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B). Consistent with data using other viruses Vlahava et al., 2021, CD107a was recirculated on a higher proportion of NK cells than IFNγ and TNFα. Nevertheless, all three markers of NK activation were significantly reduced in SARS-CoV-2 infected versus mock infected cells, suggesting that the virus has evolved to inhibit NK cell responses.
claims.evidence: This is shown by functional NK cell assays in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: CD107a was recirculated on a higher proportion of NK cells than IFNγ and TNFα.
claims.source: Consistent with data using other viruses Vlahava et al., 2021, CD107a was recirculated on a higher proportion of NK cells than IFNγ and TNFα.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the data and consistent with previous studies.

claims.claim: The virus has evolved to inhibit NK cell responses.
claims.source: Nevertheless, all three markers of NK activation were significantly reduced in SARS-CoV-2 infected versus mock infected cells, suggesting that the virus has evolved to inhibit NK cell responses.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the functional NK cell data.

claims.claim: Degranulation, IFNγ production, and TNFα production were all significantly increased in the presence of serum containing anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibodies.
claims.source: Degranulation (Figure 5A), as well as production of IFNγ (Figure 5B) and TNFα (Figure 5C), were all significantly increased in the presence of serum containing anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibodies, across a range of different NK donors (Figure 5D–F).
claims.evidence: This is shown by functional NK cell assays in Figures 5A-F.

claims.claim: ADNKA was dependent on virus replication.
claims.source: ADNKA was dependent on virus replication, since heat inactivated virus did not lead to serum-dependent NK degranulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is shown by comparing active and heat-inactivated virus in the supplementary figure.

claims.claim: NK cells were activated equivalently whether purified NK cells or PBMC were used.
claims.source: NK cells were activated equivalently whether purified NK cells or PBMC were used (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), thus these responses are due to direct stimulation of NK cells, rather than other cells responding to antibodies and releasing NK stimulating cytokines.
claims.evidence: This is shown by comparing PBMC and purified NK cells in the supplementary figure.

claims.claim: ADNKA responses are due to direct stimulation of NK cells.
claims.source: NK cells were activated equivalently whether purified NK cells or PBMC were used (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), thus these responses are due to direct stimulation of NK cells, rather than other cells responding to antibodies and releasing NK stimulating cytokines.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of PBMC and purified NK cells.

claims.claim: Viral immune evasion can be overcome through antibody dependent mechanisms.
claims.source: Viral immune evasion can therefore be overcome through antibody dependent mechanisms, suggesting that in addition to neutralising virus, SARS-CoV-2 antibodies may aid virus clearance through ADCC.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ADNKA is strong despite NK ligand downregulation.

claims.claim: SARS-CoV-2 antibodies may aid virus clearance through ADCC.
claims.source: Viral immune evasion can therefore be overcome through antibody dependent mechanisms, suggesting that in addition to neutralising virus, SARS-CoV-2 antibodies may aid virus clearance through ADCC.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the strong ADNKA responses observed.

claims.claim: The magnitude of the neutralising antibody response to SARS-CoV-2 correlates with severity of disease.
claims.source: The magnitude of the neutralising antibody response to SARS-CoV-2 correlates with severity of disease; individuals with more severe disease generate higher levels of neutralising antibody (Seow et al., 2020; Dan et al., 2021; Wajnberg et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Levels of circulating antibody can decrease over time following resolution of disease.
claims.source: Although memory B-cell responses persist, levels of circulating antibody can decrease over time following resolution of disease, such that in some mildly infected people they become undetectable after a few months (Seow et al., 2020; Dan et al., 2021; Wajnberg et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: ADNKA responses were generally of greater magnitude in individuals with more severe disease.
claims.source: ADNKA responses were generally of greater magnitude in individuals with more severe disease, with responses remaining detectable during the 150–200 day follow-up.
claims.evidence: This is shown by longitudinal serum analysis in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: Strong initial ADNKA responses were maintained over time in individuals with milder disease.
claims.source: Amongst those with milder disease, strong initial responses were maintained over time, while weaker responses decreased, becoming virtually undetectable by around 200 days.
claims.evidence: This is shown by longitudinal serum analysis in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: Weaker ADNKA responses decreased in individuals with milder disease, becoming virtually undetectable by around 200 days.
claims.source: Amongst those with milder disease, strong initial responses were maintained over time, while weaker responses decreased, becoming virtually undetectable by around 200 days.
claims.evidence: This is shown by longitudinal serum analysis in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: There was a moderate correlation between the ability of antibodies to neutralise SARS-CoV-2 and to activate ADNKA.
claims.source: There was a moderate correlation between the ability of antibodies to neutralise SARS-CoV-2, and to activate ADNKA in response to SARS-CoV-2 (Figure 5H), with a R2 value of 0.7.
claims.evidence: This is shown by correlation analysis in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: The antibodies mediating neutralisation and ADNKA may not be identical.
claims.source: Thus, although the antibodies mediating these activities may be induced in a similar manner, the antibodies mediating the two responses may not be identical.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the moderate (not perfect) correlation between neutralisation and ADNKA.

claims.claim: Substantial levels of spike protein were detected on the infected cell surface by PMP and flow cytometry.
claims.source: It is certainly a potential target during infection as, despite the fact that virion particles bud internally rather than from the cell membrane, both our PMP and flow cytometric analysis detected substantial levels of spike protein on the infected cell surface (Figure 6A, C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, D).
claims.evidence: This is shown by proteomic and flow cytometry data in the figures.

claims.claim: PMP detected membrane (M), nucleocapsid (N), ORF3a, and ORF1ab on the cell surface.
claims.source: However, our studies with other viruses have demonstrated that although viral proteins involved in virion binding and entry are found on the cell surface, and can be bound by antibody, they are not necessarily the strongest mediators of ADCC activity (Vlahava et al., 2021). PMP also detected membrane (M), nucleocapsid (N), ORF3a, and ORF1ab on the cell surface.
claims.evidence: This is shown by the proteomic data.

claims.claim: ORF1ab was only present at very low levels (1% of all viral proteins) in PMP.
claims.source: Furthermore, comparing the relative abundance of viral proteins in PMP, ORF1ab was only present at very low levels (1% of all viral proteins, significantly lower than any other SARS-CoV-2 protein).
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the proteomic data.

claims.claim: It is unlikely that any NSPs are surface-exposed.
claims.source: Taken together, it is unlikely that any NSPs are surface-exposed.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the low abundance of ORF1ab and lack of specific NSP enrichment.

claims.claim: Bioinformatic analysis revealed five additional candidate cell-surface proteins: Nsp4, Nsp6, ORF6, ORF7a, ORF7b.
claims.source: Nevertheless, we performed bioinformatic analysis of all viral proteins for the presence of potential transmembrane domains or signal peptides, revealing five additional candidate cell-surface proteins (Nsp4, Nsp6, ORF6, ORF7a, ORF7b).
claims.evidence: This is the result of bioinformatic analysis.

claims.claim: Spike primed a substantial ADNKA response when transfected into cells.
claims.source: As expected, spike primed a substantial ADNKA response.
claims.evidence: This is shown by functional NK cell assays in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Expression of ORF3a, membrane, and nucleocapsid were capable of priming ADNKA in the presence of serum containing SARS-CoV-2 antibodies.
claims.source: However, in support of our PMP data, expression of ORF3a, membrane, and nucleocapsid, were also capable of priming ADNKA in the presence of serum containing SARS-CoV-2 antibodies, while the Nsps did not.
claims.evidence: This is shown by functional NK cell assays in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The Nsps did not prime ADNKA.
claims.source: However, in support of our PMP data, expression of ORF3a, membrane, and nucleocapsid, were also capable of priming ADNKA in the presence of serum containing SARS-CoV-2 antibodies, while the Nsps did not.
claims.evidence: This is shown by functional NK cell assays in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Nucleocapsid has previously been assumed to be intracellular.
claims.source: Interestingly, nucleocapsid readily activated ADNKA despite the fact that this protein has previously been assumed to be intracellular.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge that is being challenged by the current findings.

claims.claim: ADNKA can be activated in response to levels of virus protein that are difficult to detect by flow cytometry.
claims.source: We have previously observed the exquisite sensitivity of ADNKA, which can be activated in response to levels of virus protein that are difficult to detect by flow cytometry (Vlahava et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Antigen levels can be very different in the context of virus infection compared with transfection.
claims.source: We have also shown that antigen levels can be very different in the context of virus infection, compared with transfection (Vlahava et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Nucleocapsid levels were much higher on the surface of infected cells than transfected cells.
claims.source: In support of this, nucleocapsid levels were much higher on the surface of infected cells than transfected cells (Figure 6C); detection of nucleocapsid was dependent on virus replication (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and occurred following infection of multiple different cell types (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry in Figure 6C and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Detection of nucleocapsid on the cell surface was dependent on virus replication.
claims.source: In support of this, nucleocapsid levels were much higher on the surface of infected cells than transfected cells (Figure 6C); detection of nucleocapsid was dependent on virus replication (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and occurred following infection of multiple different cell types (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is shown by comparing active and heat-inactivated virus in the supplementary figure.

claims.claim: Nucleocapsid was detected on the cell surface following infection of multiple different cell types.
claims.source: In support of this, nucleocapsid levels were much higher on the surface of infected cells than transfected cells (Figure 6C); detection of nucleocapsid was dependent on virus replication (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and occurred following infection of multiple different cell types (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry of different cell types in the supplementary figure.

claims.claim: The presence of nucleocapsid on the cell surface was supported by immunofluorescence staining of non-permeabilised infected cells.
claims.source: The presence of nucleocapsid on the cell surface was also supported by immunofluorescence staining of non-permeabilised infected cells (Figure 6D), where distinct patches of nucleocapsid were observed that sometimes, but not always, coincided with cell-cell junctions.
claims.evidence: This is shown by immunofluorescence microscopy in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Multiple proteins could be major contributors to ADCC during SARS-CoV-2 infection.
claims.source: Given how well even very low levels of surface nucleocapsid activated ADNKA, this suggested that multiple proteins could be major contributors to ADCC during SARS-CoV-2 infection.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the functional data showing multiple proteins can activate ADNKA.

claims.claim: A panel of 26 human anti-spike monoclonal antibodies was tested, including antibodies targeting the RBD, S1, NTD, and S2 domains.
claims.source: To determine the relative contribution of spike, and of different antigenic sites on spike, to ADNKA during SARS-CoV-2 infection, we tested a panel of 26 human anti-spike monoclonal antibodies, which had been isolated from naturally infected donors, and cloned as IgG1 constructs (Graham et al., 2021). The panel included antibodies targeting the RBD, S1, NTD, and S2 domains, neutralising and non-neutralising, and those targeting multiple distinct epitopes (Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental approach and is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: All 26 anti-spike antibodies bound efficiently to infected cells.
claims.source: All 26 antibodies bound efficiently to infected cells, at levels comparable to polyclonal serum (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry in the supplementary figure.

claims.claim: Only five of 26 anti-spike antibodies were capable of triggering NK cell degranulation.
claims.source: However, only five of these antibodies were capable of triggering degranulation (Figure 7A), of which two triggered TNFα (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A), and one IFNγ (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is shown by functional NK cell assays in Figure 7A and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: NK responses to anti-spike monoclonal antibodies were at dramatically lower levels than seen with polyclonal serum from a naturally infected donor.
claims.source: Importantly, these NK responses were at dramatically lower levels than seen with polyclonal serum from a naturally infected donor, even when combined (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is shown by comparing monoclonal antibodies to polyclonal serum in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: mAbs that induced ADNKA against infected cells also induced ADNKA against transfected cells.
claims.source: mAbs that induced ADNKA against infected cells also induced ADNKA against transfected cells (P008-014 and P054-044).
claims.evidence: This is shown by comparing infected and transfected cells in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Of 12 antibodies that failed to activate ADNKA against infected cells, 5 induced potent ADNKA against transfected cells.
claims.source: However, of 12 antibodies that failed to activate ADNKA against infected cells, 5 induced potent ADNKA against transfected cells.
claims.evidence: This is shown by comparing infected and transfected cells in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: The level of ADNKA induced by mAbs was extremely high against transfected cells, with many exceeding that of control seropositive serum.
claims.source: Furthermore, in contrast to infected cells, the level of ADNKA induced by mAbs was extremely high against transfected cells, with many exceeding that of our control seropositive serum.
claims.evidence: This is shown by comparing monoclonal antibodies to polyclonal serum against transfected cells in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Spike was a relatively poor ADCC target in the context of natural infection when using mAbs.
claims.source: Thus, despite a substantial ability to activate ADCC against cells transfected with spike protein, and high levels of antibody binding, spike was a relatively poor ADCC target in the context of natural infection when using mAbs.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of infected and transfected cells.

claims.claim: ELISA analysis confirmed the effective depletion of spike-specific antibodies from naturally infected sera.
claims.source: ELISA analysis confirmed the effective depletion of spike-specific antibodies (Figure 8A), which was accompanied by a significant loss of neutralisation activity (Figure 8B), across multiple donors (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This is shown by ELISA in Figure 8A.

claims.claim: Depletion of spike-specific antibodies was accompanied by a significant loss of neutralisation activity.
claims.source: ELISA analysis confirmed the effective depletion of spike-specific antibodies (Figure 8A), which was accompanied by a significant loss of neutralisation activity (Figure 8B), across multiple donors (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This is shown by neutralisation assays in Figures 8B and 8C.

claims.claim: There was no loss of ADNKA activity following spike-antibody depletion from naturally infected sera.
claims.source: However, there was no loss of ADNKA activity from any of these samples following spike-antibody depletion (Figure 8D and E), consistent with the results of our monoclonal antibody data.
claims.evidence: This is shown by ADNKA assays in Figures 8D and 8E.

claims.claim: Spike-specific antibodies dominate the neutralising antibody response but play minor roles in the ADCC response following natural infection.
claims.source: We conclude that spike-specific antibodies dominate the neutralising antibody response, but play a minor roles in the ADCC response following natural infection.
claims.evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from the antibody depletion experiments.

claims.claim: A nucleocapsid-specific human monoclonal antibody was capable of activating ADNKA against infected cells.
claims.source: A nucleocapsid-specific human monoclonal antibody was capable of activating ADNKA against infected cells (Figure 8F) and, although not to the extent of polyclonal serum, was superior to our best anti-spike antibody.
claims.evidence: This is shown by functional NK cell assays in Figure 8F.

claims.claim: The nucleocapsid-specific monoclonal antibody was superior to the best anti-spike antibody at activating ADNKA.
claims.source: A nucleocapsid-specific human monoclonal antibody was capable of activating ADNKA against infected cells (Figure 8F) and, although not to the extent of polyclonal serum, was superior to our best anti-spike antibody.
claims.evidence: This is shown by comparing the nucleocapsid and spike antibodies in Figure 8F.

claims.claim: Depletion of both spike and nucleocapsid antibodies resulted in a significant reduction in ADNKA activity.
claims.source: Furthermore, when we used the serums from which Spike antibodies had been depleted (Figure 8D–E), and also depleted anti-nucleocapsid antibodies, we saw a significant reduction in ADNKA activity (Figure 8G–H), although considerable activity remained.
claims.evidence: This is shown by ADNKA assays in Figures 8G and 8H.

claims.claim: Considerable ADNKA activity remained after depletion of both spike and nucleocapsid antibodies.
claims.source: Furthermore, when we used the serums from which Spike antibodies had been depleted (Figure 8D–E), and also depleted anti-nucleocapsid antibodies, we saw a significant reduction in ADNKA activity (Figure 8G–H), although considerable activity remained.
claims.evidence: This is shown by ADNKA assays in Figures 8G and 8H.

claims.claim: Deletion of ORF3a resulted in a small reduction (~1 log) in virus titres.
claims.source: Reagents are not available to deplete antibodies targeting ORF3a or membrane, so we instead deleted ORF3a from the virus genome. In line with existing data, this resulted in a small reduction (~1 log) in virus titres (not shown).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claims.claim: Deletion of ORF3a resulted in a small reduction in levels of spike and nucleocapsid, but not membrane.
claims.source: We therefore assessed levels of viral antigens on the cell surface following infection, which revealed that deletion of ORF3a resulted in a small reduction in levels of spike and nucleocapsid, but not membrane (Figure 8I).
claims.evidence: This is shown by flow cytometry in Figure 8I.

claims.claim: Deletion of ORF3a resulted in a dramatic reduction in ADNKA activity when using sera depleted of spike and nucleocapsid antibodies.
claims.source: To ensure that these alterations did not affect readouts, we used serums that had been depleted for antibodies targeting both Spike and Nucleocapsid, and compared ADNKA responses against wildtype or ΔORF3a virus (Figure 8J–K). Deletion of ORF3a resulted in a dramatic reduction in ADNKA activity, although this was not reduced completely to the level of seronegative serum.
claims.evidence: This is shown by ADNKA assays in Figures 8J and 8K.

claims.claim: Nucleocapsid and ORF3a are targets for ADNKA activity against SARS-CoV-2 infected cells.
claims.source: We therefore conclude that nucleocapsid and ORF3a are targets for ADNKA activity against SARS-CoV-2 infected cells, with membrane potentially also contributing.
claims.evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from the antibody depletion and virus deletion experiments.

claims.claim: Membrane potentially contributes to ADNKA activity against SARS-CoV-2 infected cells.
claims.source: We therefore conclude that nucleocapsid and ORF3a are targets for ADNKA activity against SARS-CoV-2 infected cells, with membrane potentially also contributing.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the remaining ADNKA activity after spike, nucleocapsid, and ORF3a depletion/deletion.

claims.claim: ELISA demonstrated effective depletion of spike antibodies from vaccine sera.
claims.source: As with serum from naturally infected individuals, ELISA demonstrated effective depletion of spike antibodies (Figure 9A), which was accompanied by a marked loss of virus neutralisation activity (Figure 9B and C).
claims.evidence: This is shown by ELISA in Figure 9A.

claims.claim: Depletion of spike antibodies from vaccine sera was accompanied by a marked loss of virus neutralisation activity.
claims.source: As with serum from naturally infected individuals, ELISA demonstrated effective depletion of spike antibodies (Figure 9A), which was accompanied by a marked loss of virus neutralisation activity (Figure 9B and C).
claims.evidence: This is shown by neutralisation assays in Figures 9B and 9C.

claims.claim: Vaccine sera only mediated weak ADNKA.
claims.source: In functional NK assays, these sera only mediated weak ADNKA (Figure 9D and E) and, unlike sera from naturally infected individuals, ADNKA activity was abrogated following depletion of spike antibodies.
claims.evidence: This is shown by ADNKA assays in Figures 9D and 9E.

claims.claim: ADNKA activity from vaccine sera was abrogated following depletion of spike antibodies.
claims.source: In functional NK assays, these sera only mediated weak ADNKA (Figure 9D and E) and, unlike sera from naturally infected individuals, ADNKA activity was abrogated following depletion of spike antibodies.
claims.evidence: This is shown by comparing depleted and undepleted vaccine sera in Figures 9D and 9E.

claims.claim: Vaccine mediated ADNKA was significantly weaker than responses seen following natural infection.
claims.source: When we compared responses following natural infection or vaccination, vaccine mediated ADNKA was significantly weaker than responses seen following natural infection, and was not boosted following the second dose of the vaccine (Figure 9F).
claims.evidence: This is shown by comparing vaccinated and naturally infected individuals in Figure 9F.

claims.claim: Neutralisation activity of vaccine sera was dramatically increased following the second dose.
claims.source: This was in stark contrast with the neutralisation activity of those same serum samples, which were dramatically increased following the second dose, with activity comparable to patients with severe COVID-19 disease (Figure 9G).
claims.evidence: This is shown by comparing neutralisation after first and second doses in Figure 9G.

claims.claim: Neutralisation activity after the second vaccine dose was comparable to patients with severe COVID-19 disease.
claims.source: This was in stark contrast with the neutralisation activity of those same serum samples, which were dramatically increased following the second dose, with activity comparable to patients with severe COVID-19 disease (Figure 9G).
claims.evidence: This is shown by comparing vaccinated individuals to naturally infected individuals in Figure 9G.

claims.claim: Anti-spike antibodies can mediate ADNKA, but this activity is significantly weaker than responses seen during natural infection.
claims.source: Thus, anti-spike antibodies can mediate ADNKA, but this activity is significantly weaker than responses seen during natural infection, which targets a broader repertoire of viral antigens.
claims.evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from comparing vaccine and natural infection sera.

claims.claim: ADNKA during natural infection targets a broader repertoire of viral antigens than vaccination.
claims.source: Thus, anti-spike antibodies can mediate ADNKA, but this activity is significantly weaker than responses seen during natural infection, which targets a broader repertoire of viral antigens.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the antibody depletion experiments showing non-spike antigens contribute to ADNKA.

claims.claim: SARS-CoV-2 remodelling of the plasma membrane leads to downregulation of multiple cell surface immune ligands involved with the interferon response, cytokine function, and NK activation.
claims.source: We find that SARS-CoV-2 remodelling of the plasma membrane leads to the downregulation of multiple cell surface immune ligands involved with the interferon response, cytokine function, and NK activation.
claims.evidence: This is the overall conclusion from the proteomic analysis.

claims.claim: SARS-CoV-2 remodelling may enable the virus to evade numerous effector arms of the host immune system.
claims.source: This may enable SARS-CoV-2 to evade numerous effector arms of the host immune system.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the observed downregulation of immune ligands.

claims.claim: Shutdown of host transcription and translation is likely to play a broader role in the ability of the virus to establish initial infection than previously appreciated.
claims.source: This provides an explanation for how small RNA viruses may be able to target the NK response without encoding the large repertoire of specific NK-evasins seen in the large DNA viruses (Patel et al., 2018; Berry et al., 2020), and indicates that shutdown of host transcription and translation is likely to play a broader role in the ability of the virus to establish initial infection than previously appreciated.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the mechanism of NK ligand downregulation via protein synthesis inhibition.

claims.claim: ADNKA leads to significant degranulation and production of pro-inflammatory cytokines later in disease.
claims.source: Later in disease, following the production of antibody, ADNKA leads to significant degranulation, and production of pro-inflammatory cytokines.
claims.evidence: This is shown by functional NK cell assays with seropositive sera.

claims.claim: Spike antibody is not responsible for the robust ADNKA which develops after natural infection.
claims.source: Somewhat surprisingly, spike antibody is not responsible for the robust ADNKA which develops after natural infection, and only weak ADNKA is generated following spike vaccination.
claims.evidence: This is the key finding from the antibody depletion experiments.

claims.claim: Only weak ADNKA is generated following spike vaccination.
claims.source: Somewhat surprisingly, spike antibody is not responsible for the robust ADNKA which develops after natural infection, and only weak ADNKA is generated following spike vaccination.
claims.evidence: This is shown by comparing vaccine and natural infection sera in functional assays.

claims.claim: Genetic variation in both viruses and their hosts affects the ability of viruses to modulate NK responses and influence pathogenesis.
claims.source: Genetic variation in both viruses and their hosts affects the ability of viruses to modulate NK responses, and influence pathogenesis (Patel et al., 2018; Vietzen et al., 2021a).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: SARS-CoV-2 appears to have evolved to antagonise NK activation by targeting the expression levels of multiple activating NK ligands.
claims.source: SARS-CoV-2 appears to have evolved to antagonise NK activation by targeting the expression levels of multiple activating NK ligands.
claims.evidence: This is the interpretation of the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Targeting NKG2D ligands may enable the virus to impact additional effector mechanisms beyond just NK cells.
claims.source: NKG2D is ubiquitously expressed on γδ cells and CD8+, as well as some CD4+, T-cells in addition to NK cells (Zingoni et al., 2018). Targeting NKG2D ligands may therefore enable the virus to impact additional effector mechanisms beyond just NK cells.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the known expression pattern of NKG2D.

claims.claim: MICA is particularly polymorphic with 100+ alleles.
claims.source: Amongst NKG2D ligands, MICA is particularly polymorphic (100+alleles), A549 cells express MICA*001/004 (Seidel et al., 2015), while the truncated MICA*008 is the most common allele worldwide.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: A549 cells express MICA*001/004.
claims.source: Amongst NKG2D ligands, MICA is particularly polymorphic (100+alleles), A549 cells express MICA*001/004 (Seidel et al., 2015), while the truncated MICA*008 is the most common allele worldwide.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Seidel et al., 2015.

claims.claim: The truncated MICA*008 is the most common allele worldwide.
claims.source: Amongst NKG2D ligands, MICA is particularly polymorphic (100+alleles), A549 cells express MICA*001/004 (Seidel et al., 2015), while the truncated MICA*008 is the most common allele worldwide.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about MICA alleles.

claims.claim: MICA diversity is largely driven by co-evolution of humans with virus infections.
claims.source: This diversity is largely driven by co-evolution of humans with virus infections, and reflects the broad repertoire of viral immune-evasins (Zingoni et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: MICA variation has the potential to play a role in the extremely variable outcome of SARS-CoV-2 infection.
claims.source: MICA variation therefore has the potential to play a role in the extremely variable outcome of SARS-CoV-2 infection.

results.result: Plasma membrane profiling (PMP) of SARS-CoV-2 infected AAT cells identified 4953 proteins, including 2227 plasma membrane proteins, with 914 showing significant changes. The analysis detected five viral proteins including spike, ORF3A, and membrane, and confirmed ACE2 downregulation while TMPRSS2 remained unchanged.
results.evaluation: The proteomic methodology is well-established (C43 cites previous validation), infection efficiency is demonstrated (C40), and the data quality metrics are appropriate. The findings are directly supported by the mass spectrometry data presented in figures and supplementary materials.

results.result: Interferon-stimulated genes were upregulated only at 48 hours post-infection, after viral replication is complete, indicating SARS-CoV-2 evades or suppresses IFN signaling until after virus egress. IFNAR1 downregulation at the plasma membrane represents a novel mechanism to prevent exogenous IFN signaling.
results.evaluation: The temporal clustering analysis clearly shows interferon response genes in cluster 5 (48hr upregulation), and the viral replication cycle timing is supported by citation (C51). The IFNAR1 downregulation is directly observed in the proteomic data, though the functional consequence is inferred rather than directly tested.

results.result: SARS-CoV-2 infection causes downregulation of heparan sulfate proteoglycans (syndecans, glypicans, neuropilins), which may facilitate viral egress and prevent superinfection.
results.evaluation: The downregulation is clearly shown in the proteomic data (C55), and the role of NRP1 and heparan sulfate binding is supported by citations (C56, C57). However, the proposed mechanism (C58) is speculative and not directly tested, though it is reasonably inferred by comparison to other viruses.

results.result: SARS-CoV-2 infection causes downregulation of activating NK ligands MICA, ULBP2, B7-H6, and Nectin1, while MHC-I proteins (HLA-B to HLA-E) are upregulated at 48 hours, likely due to late IFN response. The NK ligand downregulation was confirmed by flow cytometry in multiple cell types and was dependent on active viral replication.
results.evaluation: The proteomic data clearly shows NK ligand downregulation in cluster 1 (C63), confirmed by flow cytometry in multiple cell types (C65). The replication-dependence is demonstrated by heat-inactivation controls (C66). The MHC-I upregulation timing and IFN-mediated mechanism (C62) is reasonably inferred from the data and known biology.

results.result: NK ligand downregulation occurs at the level of protein synthesis rather than through intracellular retention or post-translational degradation. EndoH digestion showed no change in glycosylation patterns, proteasomal/lysosomal inhibitors did not restore NK ligand levels, and cycloheximide treatment caused rapid loss of NK ligands.
results.evaluation: The biochemical experiments provide converging evidence: EndoH sensitivity patterns are unchanged (C67), proteasomal inhibition (MG132) has no effect (C69), lysosomal inhibition (Leupeptin) shows only constitutive turnover (C70), and cycloheximide causes rapid loss (C72). These experiments collectively support synthesis-level targeting, though the mechanism is not fully elucidated.

results.result: Nsp1 and Nsp14 mediate NK ligand downregulation. Transfection of individual SARS-CoV-2 ORFs showed only Nsp1 and Nsp14 reduced NK ligand expression, with Nsp14 having stronger effects on MICA and ULBP2. Both proteins are known to inhibit host protein translation, suggesting NK ligands are highly susceptible to synthesis inhibition.
results.evaluation: The ORF screen is systematic and clearly identifies Nsp1 and Nsp14 (C73-C75). The connection to known translation inhibition functions is supported by citations (C76). However, the experiments use overexpression rather than infection context, which may not fully recapitulate the physiological mechanism. The inference about NK ligand susceptibility (C77) is reasonable but not directly proven.

results.result: NK ligand downregulation correlates with reduced NK cell activation against SARS-CoV-2 infected cells. Functional assays showed significantly reduced degranulation (CD107a), IFNγ production, and TNFα production by NK cells when co-cultured with infected versus mock-infected cells.
results.evaluation: The functional NK cell assays provide direct evidence of reduced activation across multiple markers (C79-C81). The experiments include appropriate controls and multiple donors. However, the correlation between ligand downregulation and functional outcome (C7) is not definitively proven to be causal - other viral factors could contribute to reduced NK activation.

results.result: Strong antibody-dependent NK cell activation (ADNKA) develops following SARS-CoV-2 infection, leading to high levels of degranulation and pro-inflammatory cytokine production (TNFα and IFNγ). These responses were sustained for at least 6 months in most patients, were dependent on active viral replication, and resulted from direct NK cell stimulation.
results.evaluation: The ADNKA responses are clearly demonstrated across multiple donors and timepoints (C84, C10). The replication-dependence (C85) and direct NK stimulation (C86-C87) are shown by appropriate controls (heat-inactivated virus, purified NK cells vs PBMC). The longitudinal data (C10) is well-documented in Figure 5G.

results.result: ADNKA responses were generally stronger in individuals with more severe disease and remained detectable for 150-200 days. In mild disease, strong initial responses were maintained while weaker responses declined. There was moderate correlation (R²=0.7) between neutralization and ADNKA, suggesting the antibodies mediating these responses may not be identical.
results.evaluation: The longitudinal serum analysis clearly shows disease severity-dependent patterns (C92-C94) in Figure 5G. The correlation analysis (C95) is appropriately performed and the R² value supports the conclusion that neutralizing and ADNKA antibodies are related but not identical (C96). However, the sample size for longitudinal analysis could be better specified.

results.result: Multiple SARS-CoV-2 proteins are detected on the infected cell surface and can mediate ADNKA. PMP detected spike, membrane, nucleocapsid, ORF3a, and ORF1ab, though ORF1ab was at very low levels. Transfection experiments showed spike, ORF3a, membrane, and nucleocapsid can all prime ADNKA, while NSPs cannot.
results.evaluation: The proteomic detection is direct evidence (C97-C98), and the low abundance of ORF1ab (C99) supports the conclusion that NSPs are not surface-exposed (C100). The functional transfection experiments (C102-C104) clearly demonstrate which proteins can mediate ADNKA. However, transfection may not fully recapitulate infection context, as the authors themselves note.

results.result: Nucleocapsid protein is present on the surface of SARS-CoV-2 infected cells despite being previously assumed intracellular. Surface nucleocapsid levels were much higher on infected cells than transfected cells, detection was replication-dependent, occurred across multiple cell types, and was confirmed by immunofluorescence of non-permeabilized cells.
results.evaluation: The finding is supported by multiple orthogonal approaches: flow cytometry showing higher levels on infected vs transfected cells (C108), replication-dependence (C109), multiple cell types (C110), and immunofluorescence of non-permeabilized cells (C111). This converging evidence strongly supports the surprising finding of surface nucleocapsid, though the mechanism of surface localization is not determined.

results.result: Monoclonal anti-spike antibodies are poor mediators of ADNKA against infected cells despite binding efficiently. Of 26 human anti-spike mAbs tested, only 5 triggered degranulation at dramatically lower levels than polyclonal serum. Many mAbs that failed against infected cells induced potent ADNKA against spike-transfected cells, indicating spike is a relatively poor ADCC target during natural infection.
results.evaluation: The systematic testing of 26 mAbs with diverse epitope specificities (C113) provides strong evidence. The binding data (C114) rules out lack of antibody binding as an explanation. The stark difference between infected and transfected cells (C117-C119) is clearly demonstrated and supports the conclusion (C120). However, the panel may not capture all possible spike epitopes, and the use of IgG1 constructs may not reflect natural antibody glycosylation.

results.result: Spike-specific antibodies dominate the neutralizing response but play only a minor role in ADNKA following natural infection. Depletion of spike antibodies from naturally infected sera eliminated neutralization activity but had no effect on ADNKA activity across multiple donors.
results.evaluation: The antibody depletion experiments are well-controlled with ELISA confirmation of depletion (C121) and clear demonstration of neutralization loss (C122) but no ADNKA loss (C123). The consistency across multiple donors strengthens the conclusion (C124). This is a key finding that challenges previous assumptions about spike as the dominant ADCC target.

results.result: Antibodies to nucleocapsid, ORF3a, and potentially membrane are major contributors to ADNKA during natural infection. A nucleocapsid-specific mAb activated ADNKA better than the best anti-spike mAb. Sequential depletion of spike and nucleocapsid antibodies significantly reduced ADNKA, and deletion of ORF3a from the virus further reduced ADNKA activity.
results.evaluation: The evidence is strong: nucleocapsid mAb outperforms spike mAb (C125-C126), sequential antibody depletion shows additive effects (C127-C128), and viral deletion of ORF3a reduces ADNKA (C131). The conclusion about nucleocapsid and ORF3a (C132) is well-supported, though the membrane contribution (C133) is inferred from remaining activity rather than directly demonstrated. The experiments are technically sound but the ORF3a deletion has confounding effects on other viral protein levels (C130).

results.result: ADNKA following spike vaccination is focused solely on spike, is significantly weaker than after natural infection, and is not boosted by the second dose. In contrast, neutralization activity is dramatically increased after the second dose and comparable to severe COVID-19 patients.
results.evaluation: The vaccine sera experiments clearly show spike-dependence of ADNKA (C137), weakness compared to natural infection (C138), and lack of boost after second dose (C17, C138). The contrast with neutralization (C139-C140) is striking and well-demonstrated. However, the study only examines one vaccine type (BNT162b2), limiting generalizability. The timing of sample collection relative to vaccination could also be better specified.

results.result: SARS-CoV-2 host-shutoff antagonizes innate immunity through a novel mechanism involving downregulation of multiple cell surface immune ligands. This indicates that shutdown of host transcription and translation plays a broader role in establishing infection than previously appreciated.
results.evaluation: This is a synthesis claim drawing together the NK ligand downregulation, mechanism via protein synthesis inhibition, and functional consequences. The evidence from the proteomic analysis (C143), mechanism studies (C5, C71), and functional assays (C7) collectively support this conclusion. However, the claim of novelty (C8) should be tempered - while the specific mechanism for NK ligands is new, host shutoff as an immune evasion strategy is well-known.

results.result: The ability of monoclonal spike antibodies to bind infected cells does not correlate with ADNKA activity, indicating that epitope, position, or binding angle is critical. Notably, 4/5 ADNKA-activating anti-spike antibodies bound the NTD, suggesting this site may be structurally advantageous for Fc-mediated responses.
results.evaluation: The lack of correlation between binding and function (C175) is clearly demonstrated in the data. The observation about NTD-binding antibodies (C177) is factual, though the sample size is small (5 antibodies). The inference about structural advantage (C178) is reasonable speculation but not proven. This result provides important insights for antibody therapeutic development.

results.result: This work identifies a potential functional role for antibodies targeting nucleocapsid, ORF3a, and membrane during natural SARS-CoV-2 infection for the first time, suggesting these immunodominant targets are major contributors to ADCC.
results.evaluation: The functional experiments clearly demonstrate ADCC activity mediated by antibodies to these proteins (C14, C132). The claim of novelty (C182) appears justified as previous ADCC studies focused on spike. However, the authors should acknowledge that antibody responses to these proteins were already known to exist - the novelty is in demonstrating their functional role in ADCC.

results.result: Viral immune evasion of NK cells can be overcome through antibody-dependent mechanisms, suggesting SARS-CoV-2 antibodies may aid virus clearance through ADCC in addition to neutralization.
results.evaluation: While the data clearly show that ADNKA can overcome the NK ligand downregulation (C88 is supported), the speculation about aiding virus clearance (C89) is not directly tested. The study demonstrates ADNKA activity in vitro but does not provide evidence for actual viral clearance or in vivo relevance. This would require additional experiments such as viral load measurements or animal studies.

results.result: ADNKA may contribute to immunopathology in severe COVID-19 through high levels of TNFα and IFNγ production, activation of myeloid cells and complement. TNFα and IFNγ correlate with severe disease, and critically ill patients have higher proportions of afucosylated antibodies that may promote stronger ADCC. A skewed spike:nucleocapsid antibody ratio is associated with severe disease.
results.evaluation: The speculation about immunopathology (C165, C187, C190) is based on observed cytokine production and correlations from the literature (C166, C167, C186) but is not directly tested in this study. The authors appropriately present this as speculation, but the causal relationship between ADNKA and disease severity is not established. The observation that all mild/asymptomatic patients also developed strong ADNKA (C192) actually argues against a simple pathogenic role.

results.result: Virus variants may evolve to evade ADCC responses as mutations in membrane, ORF3a, and nucleocapsid can reduce antibody binding. Including nucleocapsid in vaccines could engage broader immune effector pathways and improve efficacy against viral variants.
results.evaluation: The observation that variants contain mutations in ADCC target proteins (C193-C194) is factual and cited. However, the speculation about immune evasion (C195) and vaccine improvement (C196-C198) is not tested. While the logic is sound, demonstrating that these mutations actually reduce ADCC and that nucleocapsid inclusion would improve vaccine efficacy would require additional experiments. This represents reasonable future directions rather than supported conclusions.
